implementation_notes: A Scala 3 export clause defines aliases for selected members of a stable path, and a renaming selector (x as y) supplies the intention-revealing name: export delegate.{cancel as cancelOrder} gives callers cancelOrder with no method body anywhere, which is the pattern realized by the language instead of by a hand-written one-liner. The reference notes the aliases are always final - they cannot be overridden and cannot override concrete members of base classes - so use export when the delegated surface should be closed, and fall back to a hand-written def when a subclass must change the behaviour or when the alias should carry its own Scaladoc.
code_sketch:
final class OrderService(delegate: OrderRepository):
  export delegate.{cancel as cancelOrder, count as orderCount}
pitfalls: Export aliases are final and cannot override concrete members inherited from a base class, so a delegating class designed for extension must write plain defs instead.
A wildcard export (export delegate.*) republishes everything the path exposes, including members exported from elsewhere, silently widening the class's API and its binary surface.
Aliases are compiler-generated members: their Scaladoc and parameter names come from the aliased definition, so published documentation can describe an operation under the delegate's own wording.

variants.name: Hand-written one-line def (Scala 2.13)
variants.implementation_notes: Before Scala 3, and wherever a member must be overridable or documented, the delegating method is written by hand with an expression body: def cancelOrder(id: OrderId): CancelResult = delegate.cancel(id). There is no export clause on Scala 2, and trait-based delegation by self-type or abstract override adds machinery for the same one-line result, so the plain def stays the honest choice; the compiler inlines it freely because the class and the delegate are known types.
pitfalls: Implicit-conversion delegation (the pre-Scala 3 facade style) needs scala.language.implicitConversions, surprises readers, and is deprecated in Scala 3 - do not build one-line forwarding on implicits.
The expression body infers the type from the delegate; widening the delegate's return type silently changes the wrapper's public signature, so annotate return types on published members.
